title: Contingency Playbook for SLO Regressions and Silent Degradations
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview

This playbook defines the detection, triage, containment, and communication patterns for SLO regressions and 'silent degradations' — situations where customer-visible quality or latency degrades without a clear outage or error spike. This doc focuses on infra, serving runtime, and model-routing mitigations and includes on-call handoff checklists and a customer-facing status page template tailored for slow degradations.

Scope

- Services: inference runtime (api-server, grpc-proxy, kv-cache), model-routing layer, caching/prefix store, and observability pipelines (metrics/traces).
- Not covered: billing anomalies, planned maintenance (see maintenance-runbook).

Definitions

- SLO regression: measurable breach of a configured SLO (latency / error / availability) for a sustained window.
- Silent degradation: degradation in throughput/latency or quality that does not trigger primary alerts (e.g., p50 stable, p99 slowly drifting, model output quality subtlety).
- Escalation owner: primary on-call for the impacted service; fallback is SRE rotation lead.

Detection signals and examples

Operators should consider multiple weak signals together rather than a single alert. Typical signals: 

1. Latency drift (tail): p99(latency) increases by > 30% for 15m while p50 changes < 10%.

Example PromQL: 
- p99: "histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, service))"
- drift rule alert (suggested): "WHEN (p99 / p99_baseline) > 1.30 FOR 15m"

2. KV/cache miss rate rising: prefix_cache_miss_ratio increases > 10 percentage points from baseline for 10m.

PromQL: "(sum(prefix_cache_misses) / sum(prefix_cache_requests))"

3. Model quality drift: eval-set score drop (BLEU/EM/RoBERTa-score) or rise in rerank mismatch. These are often surfaced by offline eval jobs; integrate alerting if a rolling-window drop > 3 stddevs.

4. Increased tail CPU/Latency on GPU hosts: hours-long tail latencies correlated with host-side GPU throttling or OOM logs.

5. Observability pipeline lag: traces/metrics ingestion delay causing stale dashboards (checkhousekeeping: observability_forwarder_enqueue_seconds > 20s).

Immediate triage checklist (first 15 minutes)

1) Acknowledge and annotate the alert in incident tool.
2) Establish impact: check customer-facing SLOs, error budget burn rate, and whether the degradation affects a single region/cluster or global. Query:
- "select sum(requests) by (region) where latency>threshold" (use internal queries).

3) Quick isolation attempts (parallel):
- Check model-routing: are requests being routed to a new model variant? (Console > Routing > recent rollouts).
- Check cache KPIs: hit rate, eviction rate, and KV store latency.
- Check host-level metrics: GPU/utilization, CPU steal, and network egress latencies.

4) If quality regression suspected, pull a quick sample set of 30 requests across recent 30 minutes and run against golden prompt-set. Capture diffs. Use CLI: 
- curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_TOKEN" https://api.redwood/models/{model}/logs?since=30m | jq '.samples[0:30]' > /tmp/samples.json

5) Decide: mitigation vs longer investigation. If impact affects customers or SLO risk > 10% of error budget, escalate per ladder below.

Containment and automated mitigations

When quick isolation indicates a likely cause, prefer gradual, reversible mitigations: 

- Route around: apply model-variant routing to a stable variant (canary rollback). Example command snippet: 
  - redwood routing set-weights --route inference-prod --variant stable-v2=1.0 --variant canary=0.0 --reason "auto-contain-slo-drift"

- Increase cache TTLs and enable cold-warm session pooling to reduce tail pressure.

- Reduce batch window or force single-request mode for critical low-latency customers. CLI: 
  - redwood runtime update --service api-server --param batching.max_ms=0 --reason "reduce-tail-latency"

- Scale up dedicated pool or evict noisy tenants (if within Dedicated). Runbook snippet: 
  - eskalate to capacity lead, add 2x instances to the dedicated pool, observe 10m.

Escalation ladder (single-line table)

Owner -> Role -> Escalation criteria
Primary on-call -> Service owner (SRE/infra) -> Any sustained SLO regression > 15m or customer-impacting
Secondary on-call -> Team lead -> Primary unavailable OR cross-service correlation present
Platform Reliability -> SRE Manager -> Multi-region or >20% error budget burn
Security -> SecOps -> if instrumentation shows tampering or data leakage indicators
Eng Leadership -> VP Eng -> Major customers degraded or regulatory exposure

Communication templates

Status page short (public) — use when customers may notice performance degradation: 

Title: "Performance degradation affecting inference latency (partial)"
Status: "Investigating"
Impact: "Some requests in US-west and EU regions are experiencing higher than normal tail latency. No request errors or data loss observed."
Customer guidance: "We are routing traffic to stable model variants and scaling pools to improve latency. No action required. We will provide updates every 30 minutes."
Estimated next update: "+30 minutes"

Status page internal (detailed):
- Start time: 2026-03-01T10:12:00Z
- Affected regions: us-west-2, eu-central-1
- Observed signal: p99(latency) +45% vs baseline, prefix_cache_miss_rate +12pp
- Mitigations applied: model routing rollback to stable-v2 at 10:21Z, increased cache TTLs at 10:25Z, added 2 instances to dedicated pool at 10:30Z
- Next steps: validate p99 for 30m before removing "investigating" status

Customer email template (short):

Subject: "Update: Performance degradation affecting inference latency"
Body: "Hello — We are investigating increased latency affecting requests in some regions. We have applied mitigations (routing to stable variants and scaling capacity). There is no data loss and no action is required on your side. We will send another update in 30 minutes or when we have a resolution."

On-call shift and handoff checklist (for this class of incident)

- At start of shift: verify alerts are healthy, run the 5-min synthetic test against primary regions, and confirm cache hit rates are within expected range.
- When taking an incident: update the incident entry with a short runbook link and triage notes.
- Before handing off: ensure the next on-call has:
  1. Summary of detection signals and baseline queries.
  2. List of mitigations tried and their timestamps.
  3. Remaining action items and who owns them.
  4. Evidence artifacts: sample inputs/outputs, Prometheus graphs (links), and logs archive location.

Post-incident: analysis and guardrail improvements

1) Postmortem within 72 hours: owner must create an incident postmortem linking to this playbook. Include: root cause hypothesis, timeline, mitigations, and measurable actions.
2) Immediate guardrail candidates: 
   - Add composite alert that combines p99 drift and cache miss ratio so slow degradations surface earlier.
   - Add a scheduled eval job that runs a compact prompt set every 10 minutes for critical models and surface drift alerts when score drops > 2% absolute.
   - Implement a low-latency synthetic user endpoint with injected prompt-set to surface tail drift.

Game-day exercise (90 min template)

Objective: Validate detection of slow tail latency increase and the team's ability to route to stable variants without customer impact.

Agenda: 
- 0-10m: Briefing and assign roles (comm lead, mitigation lead, routing engineer, SRE).
- 10-30m: Inject synthetic tail latency by adding artificial sleep to a canary model replica (simulated).
- 30-60m: Team must detect drift using dashboards/alerts and apply routing rollback.
- 60-80m: Validate customer-facing status update and confirm metrics recovery.
- 80-90m: Retro and action assignment.

Success criteria: detection within 20 minutes of injection, rollback without dropping throughput for high-tier customers, and <5 minutes of customer-visible elevated latency after rollback.

Ownership and SLAs

- Primary owner: inference-sre@redwood (on-call).
- Secondary owner: platform-ops@redwood.
- SLA notes: When a silent degradation impacts >5% of requests for >15m, the incident should be treated as Sev2 for internal reporting and postmortem requirements.

Appendix: example alerts and queries

- Composite drift alert (pseudo-YAML):
  - name: slo-drift-composite
    expr: |
      (histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, service)) / p99_baseline) > 1.30 and (prefix_cache_miss_ratio - baseline_cache_miss) > 0.10
    for: 15m
    labels: {severity: warning, owner: inference-sre}

- Quick CLI snippets: 
  - sample extraction: 
    curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_TOKEN" 
      "https://internal-api.redwood/v1/logs?service=inference-prod&since=30m&limit=100" | jq '.entries' > /tmp/incident-samples.json

- Evidence artifact naming convention: "incident-<YYYYMMDD>-<short-id>-evidence.tar.gz"

Notes and change history

- 2025-11-12 A. Patel - initial draft
- 2026-03-01 A. Patel - added composite alert examples, game-day template, and customer templates

If unsure during triage, call the SRE escalation channel (#sre-escalations) and follow the escalation ladder above. This playbook is a living document: add new signals and mitigation patterns as we learn from postmortems.
